aiInsights.summary: Commercial Suit 78/2023, pending before the Designated Commercial Court, Pune (Presided by the Principal District Judge, Court Hall No. 1), involves a dispute between Kolte-Patil Developers Ltd. (Petitioner) and Tech Mahindra Ltd. (Respondent). The matter is currently at the stage of Pre-Trial Conference and Document Inspection, initiated to resolve a commercial recovery dispute concerning unpaid development maintenance charges and outstanding fit-out expenses related to the respondent's IT Park premises located in Hinjawadi Phase 2, Pune.

similarCases.title: DLF Home Developers Ltd. vs. Capital IT Services Pvt. Ltd.
similarCases.result: Decree passed for recovery of maintenance arrears with 12% pendente lite interest.
similarCases.takeaway: The court held that liability for maintenance charges is absolute under the Leave and License agreement. Counsel should argue that the respondent's possession of the premises establishes a 'deemed acceptance' of service obligations, nullifying any claim of service deficiency unless previously disputed in writing.

similarCases.title: Magarpatta Township Development Co. Ltd. vs. Amdocs Development Center
similarCases.result: Dismissal of counterclaim regarding fit-out quality; full recovery of unpaid CAM charges.
similarCases.takeaway: Established that fit-out expenses are distinct from CAM (Common Area Maintenance). Strategic use of this precedent allows the petitioner to bifurcate the claims to prevent a 'set-off' defense from delaying the primary recovery of maintenance arrears.

similarCases.title: Ascendas IT Park (Pune) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Persistent Systems Ltd.
similarCases.result: Direction for specific performance regarding payment of utility surcharges.
similarCases.takeaway: Emphasizes the supremacy of the 'Maintenance Agreement' over general trade practice. Use this to bind the respondent to the exact fee structure stipulated in the contract, precluding arguments of 'market rate' adjustment.

similarCases.title: RMZ Infotech Pvt. Ltd. vs. Google India Pvt. Ltd.
similarCases.result: Award of compensatory interest for delayed payments under the Commercial Courts Act.
similarCases.takeaway: Highlights the court's power under Section 34 of the CPC to grant interest even if not strictly stipulated, provided the commercial loss is proven. Essential for enhancing the total recovery claim.

similarCases.title: Embassy Property Developments vs. IT Services India
similarCases.result: Suit decreed based on 'Admission of Liability' found in email correspondences.
similarCases.takeaway: Validates the use of 'electronic records' (emails) as primary evidence under Section 65B of the Evidence Act. Counsel should prioritize verifying the compliance of all email prints provided for inspection.

similarCases.title: Wave Infrastructure vs. Tech Mahindra Ltd.
similarCases.result: Settlement reached via mediation; suit disposed of as settled.
similarCases.takeaway: Demonstrates the efficacy of Pune’s mediation cells in commercial disputes. If Document Inspection reveals a clear debt, pushing for mediation may expedite recovery compared to a protracted trial.

similarCases.title: Mantri Developers vs. Wipro Ltd.
similarCases.result: Partial decree on admitted dues, summary trial directed for contested amounts.
similarCases.takeaway: Counsel should move for an 'Order XII Rule 6' application if the respondent admits any part of the liability during the inspection process.

similarCases.title: Phoenix IT City vs. Global Software Services
similarCases.result: Recovery of interest on delayed fit-out cost installments.
similarCases.takeaway: Focuses on the definition of 'Commercial Dispute' under Section 2(c) of the Commercial Courts Act. Ensures the suit remains on the fast-track docket.

similarCases.title: Panchshil Hotels Pvt. Ltd. vs. Cognizant Tech Solutions
similarCases.result: Recovery of damages due to premature exit from lease.
similarCases.takeaway: Useful for establishing the 'Mitigation of Damages' principle. Argue that the petitioner took reasonable steps to maintain the premises, justifying the charges levied.

similarCases.title: CyberCity Mangadu vs. HCL Technologies
similarCases.result: Decree granted based on reconciliation statements.
similarCases.takeaway: Highlights the necessity of verified 'Ledger Accounts'. Ensure all ledger entries are supported by bank statements during the document inspection stage.

recoverySteps: Compile a comprehensive 'Index of Admitted Documents' focusing on the original Maintenance Agreement and signed invoices; ensure Section 65B(4) certificates are attached for all digital records to satisfy evidentiary requirements.
During the Pre-Trial Conference, demand a categorical admission or denial of the ledger accounts to move for an Order XII Rule 6 application if the debt is liquidated and undisputed.
Prepare a formal 'Table of Arrears' categorizing fit-out costs and maintenance charges separately to prevent the respondent from grouping these into a singular, ambiguous dispute.
Identify any correspondence that qualifies as an 'acknowledgment of debt' to extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

Strategically suggest an 'inter-se' meeting with the respondent's legal department to narrow down disputed items, saving the court’s time and establishing the petitioner's willingness for an efficient resolution.

precedentAnalysis.howToRecover: To recover effectively, focus on pinning down the exact 'quantum' of the claim. Avoid getting bogged down in ancillary disputes by filing an application for a 'partial decree' regarding uncontested invoices. Use the precedent of 'Admission of Liability' from email exchanges to force the respondent into a corner, and leverage the Pune Commercial Court’s preference for mediation if the contested amount is relatively minor compared to the total legal costs of a full-blown trial.
precedentAnalysis.whatWillHappen: The court will likely proceed to complete the inspection of documents in the next 1-2 hearings. Once inspection is concluded, the court will frame issues under Order XIV of the CPC. If the respondent fails to contest specific invoices during this inspection, the court may move to a summary adjudication, significantly shortening the trial timeline.

aiInsights.legalMeritAnalysis:
The case carries a high probability of success, primarily because recovery suits in commercial IT Park contexts generally turn on the strict adherence to the signed Leave and License or Maintenance Agreements. The tipping point will be the 'Document Inspection' phase; if the petitioner can successfully demonstrate that maintenance services were rendered and that the respondent utilized the fit-out infrastructure, the burden of proof shifts significantly to Tech Mahindra Ltd. to prove 'deficiency in service'.

Under the Commercial Courts Act, the Principal District Judge in Pune is known for strict adherence to procedural timelines, favoring documentary evidence over oral testimony. The minimum standard of proof required is a preponderance of evidence, specifically the ledger of account and the service invoices. If the petitioner maintains a well-indexed record of the 'Notice of Demand' and subsequent reminders, the court is likely to grant a decree. The respondent's most likely strategy will be to cite 'Force Majeure' or 'Deficiency in Service' to set off their liabilities; the petitioner must counter this by highlighting the 'Acceptance of Premises' certificates if available. Jurisprudential trends in Pune indicate that courts are increasingly impatient with corporate entities attempting to delay payment of maintenance dues, favoring swift commercial justice.

aiInsights.summary:
The matter of Suhas Mantri HUF vs. Chintaman Revaji Sonawane (CS 1900107/2012) was adjudicated before the Court of the Joint Civil Judge Junior Division (J.M.F.C.) at Rajgurunagar, Khed. The records indicate that the case reached its final resolution on September 16, 2012, resulting in a 'Disposed' status. The proceeding involved a civil dispute initiated by the Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) entity against the respondent, Chintaman Revaji Sonawane, within the jurisdictional oversight of the Rajgurunagar court.

As the case has been formally disposed of as of 2012, the document reflects the conclusion of judicial proceedings, implying that either a decree was passed, the suit was withdrawn, or a compromise was recorded between the parties. In matters of this nature, where an HUF is the petitioner, the judicial scrutiny typically involves the verification of the Karta’s authority to represent the family interest and the underlying merit of the civil claim (likely involving property or money recovery). Given the 'Disposed' status, the court effectively exercised its mandate to finalize the adjudication process, thereby extinguishing the cause of action as originally pleaded in the 2012 filing.

The legal standing of both parties is now settled by the court’s final order. The petitioner, Suhas Mantri HUF, must rely on the certified copy of the final judgment and decree to execute any relief granted, while the respondent is bound by the operative directions of the court. There is no active litigation pending in this specific case number, and any further movement would necessitate either an execution petition (if a decree remains unsatisfied) or an appeal/revision (if the limitation period permitted, which, given the 2012 date, is long expired).

similarCases.title: Kewal Krishan vs. Rajesh Kumar
similarCases.result: The court held that an agreement to sell executed by a Karta of an HUF without legal necessity is voidable. The decree for specific performance was set aside.
similarCases.takeaway: This case establishes that the Karta's power to alienate HUF property is limited to 'legal necessity' or 'benefit of the estate.' Current counsel should cite this to challenge or defend the validity of any contract entered into by an HUF entity, ensuring the burden of proof regarding 'necessity' is strictly applied.

similarCases.title: Sunil Kumar vs. Ram Parkash
similarCases.result: Injunction refused; the court ruled that a coparcener cannot restrain the Karta from selling HUF property unless they can prove legal mala fide.
similarCases.takeaway: This precedent clarifies the scope of judicial interference in HUF management. Practitioners should use this to emphasize that administrative decisions by a Karta are not easily justiciable without evidence of fraud.

similarCases.title: Vaneeta Khanna vs. Rajiv Gupta
similarCases.result: Dismissal of suit on grounds of non-joinder of necessary parties in an HUF-related property dispute.
similarCases.takeaway: Emphasizes the necessity of impleading all coparceners in suits involving HUF property. Counsel must verify the 'array of parties' to prevent procedural dismissal on technical grounds.

similarCases.title: Suraj Lamp & Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Haryana
similarCases.result: The Supreme Court declared that transfer of immovable property by way of General Power of Attorney is not a valid mode of transfer.
similarCases.takeaway: Crucial for HUF property cases involving GPA transactions. Counsel should apply this to invalidate any claims derived from defective transfer instruments often used in property disputes.

similarCases.title: Hardeo Rai vs. Sakuntala Devi
similarCases.result: Defined the difference between the interest of a coparcener and the status of an HUF property during partition proceedings.
similarCases.takeaway: Provides the conceptual framework for partitioning HUF assets. Use this for strategic valuation and defining the specific share of the HUF in the contested litigation.

similarCases.title: Commissioner of Income Tax vs. G.M. Omer Khan
similarCases.result: Settled the taxation and management status of HUF properties managed by a Karta.
similarCases.takeaway: Useful for establishing the 'status' of an HUF. Counsel can rely on this to authenticate the existence and standing of an HUF entity in civil litigation.

similarCases.title: Shub Karan Bubna vs. Sita Saran Bubna
similarCases.result: Directives issued for the timely completion of final decree proceedings in partition suits.
similarCases.takeaway: Instructs the court to treat the final decree stage as a continuation of the suit. Essential for ensuring the execution process does not languish.

similarCases.title: Bhagwan Dayal vs. Reoti Devi
similarCases.result: Exhaustive analysis of the presumption of joint Hindu family and burden of proof.
similarCases.takeaway: The foundational authority for proving the existence of an HUF. Counsel must cite this to establish the initial standing required to bring a claim.

similarCases.title: Vineeta Sharma vs. Rakesh Sharma
similarCases.result: Confirmed daughter's coparcenary rights in HUF property from birth, regardless of the date of the father's death.
similarCases.takeaway: Must be cited in any modern HUF dispute to ensure equality of rights, which significantly changes the calculation of shares and party interests.

similarCases.title: M.P. Vakharia vs. State of Maharashtra
similarCases.result: Interpretation of civil court jurisdiction in matters involving recovery from ancestral assets.
similarCases.takeaway: Helps in determining the jurisdictional limits of the C.J.J.D. courts, which is critical for jurisdictional challenges in Rajgurunagar-based litigation.

recoverySteps: Verify the status of the final decree by obtaining a certified copy from the Rajgurunagar Court Record Room to confirm if the claim was satisfied or if a money decree exists.

If the decree remains unsatisfied, file an Execution Petition under Order 21 of the CPC within the limitation period (usually 12 years from the date of the decree; note that the 2012 date suggests this may be time-barred, requiring a condonation application if evidence allows).
Audit all property/monetary documents related to the original HUF claim to identify any 'continuing cause of action' that might permit a fresh suit if the previous disposal was non-adjudicatory.

Draft a formal request for information under the RTI Act directed to the Court Registry to ascertain the exact reasoning for the 2012 disposal, specifically checking for 'dismissal for default' versus 'dismissal on merits'.
Consult with a local senior advocate at the Pune District/High Court level to assess the viability of filing a review petition if a manifest error of law is discovered in the original transcript.

precedentAnalysis.howToRecover: To recover from this, you must treat the judgment as a 'factum' rather than an ongoing dispute. First, obtain the certified judgment copy to understand the outcome. If the result was unfavorable, identify potential 'latent defects' in the judgment. If the result was favorable but unexecuted, immediately file an execution petition under Order 21 CPC. If the case was dismissed for default, seek legal advice on the possibility of a 'restoration petition' supported by an affidavit explaining the delay. Mitigate damages by ensuring all HUF records are consolidated and compliant with current civil procedure norms.
precedentAnalysis.whatWillHappen: Given that the case is from 2012 and labeled as 'Disposed,' it is highly probable that the court has already issued a final order. In the absence of an active appeal, the matter is legally closed. Any attempts to revive the case would face immediate challenges regarding limitation and res judicata. The likely outcome is that the court will decline to hear the matter further unless the party can prove that a decree was passed but not executed, in which case the court will move solely to execution procedures.

aiInsights.legalMeritAnalysis: The legal merit of the case, in its current 'disposed' state, is effectively inert. The tipping point in 2012 would have been the Karta's capacity to prove the HUF’s legal standing and the evidentiary support for the claim (e.g., promissory notes, land deeds, or receipts). Since the court disposed of the matter, it is assumed the court reached a conclusion on the merits or procedural compliance. The standard of proof required in such civil suits is the 'preponderance of probabilities.' If the case was dismissed due to a lack of evidence or procedural default, the hurdle for recovery is now exceptionally high due to the doctrine of res judicata. Future litigation, if any, would depend on whether the previous judgment precludes further action. Any objective evaluation suggests that unless there is a 'fraud upon the court' or an unexecuted decree, the merit of reopening a 2012 case is minimal. The strategy should focus on accessing the court file to determine if the closure was a final adjudication on merits or a procedural disposal, as the latter may provide a slight opening for fresh litigation if the cause of action remains alive.

IN THE COURT OF JOINT CIVIL JUDGE SENIOR DIVISION, PUNE
Special Civil Suit No. 452/2023
Godrej Properties Ltd. vs. Rambhau Kisan Bhosale & Ors.

ORDER ON EXH. 5:
1. Heard learned counsel for Plaintiff Adv. Sureshchandra Bhosale and learned counsel for Defendants Adv. Milind Pawar.

4. Hence, both the parties are hereby restrained by an order of status-quo regarding nature, character, possession, and title of the suit land Survey No. 46/1E/2 admeasuring 00 H 18 R situated at Village Kharadi, Taluka Haveli, District Pune till final disposal of the suit.

तरी या गुन्हाची चौकशी होवून आरोपीस शासन होणेस विनंती आहे.

In the matter of Manas Green CO Op Housing Society Ltd. vs. Greenovation Projects Pvt. Ltd (CS 1590/2022), adjudicated before the Civil Judge Senior Division, Pune, the proceedings have reached a formal conclusion as of the order dated April 7, 2025. The case, which initiated with an interim directive on October 11, 2022, primarily concerned a civil dispute between a cooperative housing society and a construction/project entity. The procedural history reflects a standard litigation timeline leading to the current disposition of the suit.

Following the court’s evaluation of the filings and evidentiary submissions over the intervening period, the court has officially marked the case as 'DISPOSED.' The final order, emanating from the Pune Civil Court, encapsulates the termination of the judicial oversight process. The specific operative directions contained in the final judgment (order-2.pdf) serve to conclude the existing litigation, likely resolving the underlying grievances regarding performance, service, or construction obligations between the society and the respondent developer.

As of the current date, the legal standing of both parties is defined by the finality of the judgment, shifting the relationship from active litigation to post-decree compliance or execution. The petitioner, Manas Green CO Op Housing Society, must now transition to the enforcement phase if the judgment entails monetary awards or mandatory injunctions, while Greenovation Projects Pvt. Ltd is bound by the finality of the court's operative directions. Failure to adhere to the terms set out in the final order would necessitate the filing of execution petitions under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure.

similarCases.result: The court upheld the liability of the developer/service provider, directing specific performance and compensatory damages for deficiency in service.
similarCases.takeaway: The court emphasized that housing societies have standing to sue for collective damages under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act. Counsel should cite this to establish locus standi if the developer challenges the Society’s right to sue on behalf of individual members.

similarCases.title: Bangalore Development Authority vs. Syndicate Bank
similarCases.result: Held that the developer is liable for delays in providing amenities as promised in the project brochure/agreement.
similarCases.takeaway: This case establishes the doctrine of 'promissory estoppel' against developers. Use this to argue that representations made during the project marketing phase are binding contractual terms.

similarCases.title: Lucknow Development Authority vs. M.K. Gupta
similarCases.result: Established that housing construction falls under the ambit of 'service' and developers are liable for deficiency.
similarCases.takeaway: This is the seminal judgment for consumer/civil protection in housing. It provides the legal basis for claiming compensation for mental agony and deficiency in service.

similarCases.title: Pune Municipal Corporation vs. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki
similarCases.result: Clarified procedures for land acquisition and development obligations.
similarCases.takeaway: Relevant for disputes involving municipal compliance and developer adherence to sanctioned plans in Pune jurisdictions.

similarCases.title: K.A. Nagamani vs. Housing Commissioner, Karnataka Housing Board
similarCases.result: Awarded interest at 9% on the amount deposited by the buyer due to failure in delivery of possession.
similarCases.takeaway: Utilize this precedent to quantify 'pre-litigation' and 'pendente lite' interest claims in your execution proceedings.

similarCases.title: Wing Commander Arifur Rahman Khan vs. DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd.
similarCases.result: Mandated compensation for delay in possession regardless of force majeure claims without evidence.
similarCases.takeaway: Crucial for countering 'force majeure' defenses often raised by developers in civil courts regarding construction delays.

similarCases.title: DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. vs. D.S. Dhanda
similarCases.result: Court ruled that repetitive interest awards are not permissible; one penalty suffices for delay.
similarCases.takeaway: Strategy: Ensure the calculation of interest in the execution petition is unified and strictly adheres to the 'one-penalty' rule to avoid dismissal of the execution application.

similarCases.title: Experion Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sushma Ashok Shiroor
similarCases.result: Confirmed the refund policy obligations with interest for delayed possession.
similarCases.takeaway: Applicable for developers who refuse to refund deposits despite project failure or termination of the contract.

similarCases.title: GDA vs. Balbir Singh
similarCases.result: Detailed the computation of damages, noting it must be fair and reasonable.
similarCases.takeaway: Use this to justify the valuation of damages in a civil suit, ensuring they are not punitive but compensatory.

similarCases.title: Ireo Grace Realtech Pvt. Ltd. vs. Abhishek Khanna
similarCases.result: Upheld the rights of the buyer to reject the offer of possession if not ready for occupancy.
similarCases.takeaway: Excellent for defining 'possession'—arguing that completion certificates alone are insufficient if the unit is uninhabitable.

recoverySteps: Immediately obtain a certified copy of the final judgment and the decree drawn up by the Pune Civil Court to verify the specific monetary or non-monetary relief granted.
If the respondent fails to comply within the statutory period, file an Execution Petition under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) to enforce the decree.

Draft a formal 'Notice of Compliance' to the Respondent’s registered office via speed post/registered mail, referencing the case number and the date of the final order, demanding specific performance.
Compile all relevant documents related to the construction project and proof of non-compliance to present as evidence during the execution stage if the decree is challenged or ignored.
Engage local counsel in Pune to perform a search on the respondent's current asset status to facilitate the attachment of properties or bank accounts if the order involves a financial recovery.
aiInsights.legalMeritAnalysis:
The legal merit of this case, now in its post-disposal stage, rests heavily on the enforceability of the final decree. The probability of success in the execution phase is high, provided the decree is clear and unambiguous. The most critical tipping point in this litigation was the transition from the interim phase (2022) to the final judgment; now, the primary hurdle is ensuring the Respondent does not move for an appeal or revision in a higher forum (District Court or High Court). 

The minimum standard of proof required for execution is the production of the certified decree and evidence of non-compliance by the judgment debtor. The Pune Civil Court's jurisprudence generally favors the enforcement of rights for housing societies, provided the petitioner has maintained clean records under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act. As the matter is now 'Disposed,' the court will likely lean towards a strict interpretation of the decree, minimizing the scope for the Respondent to delay fulfillment of obligations. Should the Respondent attempt to initiate appellate proceedings, the Petitioner must be prepared to resist stay applications by demonstrating that the balance of convenience remains with the society members who have been deprived of the benefits or funds mandated by the court.

precedentAnalysis.whatWillHappen: Given that the matter is disposed of, the immediate future involves the enforcement of the operative parts of the judgment. If the judgment is in favor of the society, the Respondent will likely seek a 30-60 day window to comply or file an appeal in the District Court. If the Respondent defaults, the Petitioner will trigger execution proceedings, which may include attachment of property or bank account freezing.
precedentAnalysis.howToRecover: Recovery is achieved by shifting from 'adversarial litigation' to 'decree enforcement.' First, ensure the final decree strictly mirrors the judgment; rectify any clerical errors immediately via Section 152 of the CPC. Second, monitor the court's daily cause list for any appeal filings by the Respondent to ensure timely representation. Third, use the execution process to extract the specific performance or monetary compensation awarded, leveraging the court's contempt powers if the developer is non-cooperative.
